concepts.title: Writing a dynamite introduction
concepts.one_liner: A dynamite introduction must clearly state what the paper is about, the problem it solves, why it is interesting, what is new, and why it is neat.
concepts.content: Regarding paper introductions, Kajiya writes, "You must make your paper easy to read. You've got to make it easy for anyone to tell what your paper is about, what problem it solves, why the problem is interesting, what is really new in your paper (and what isn't), why it's so neat. And you must do it up front. In other words, you must write a dynamite introduction."
concepts.motivation_md: The introduction is the first thing a reader encounters. If it fails to immediately communicate the paper's value and novelty, the reader may lose interest before reaching the core contributions.
concepts.recap_md: - Make the paper easy to read by stating the problem and solution up front.

concepts.title: Visualizing the main idea
concepts.one_liner: Showing a simple example that captures the main idea of a paper can be very helpful for reader comprehension.
concepts.content: When appropriate to the paper, it can be very helpful to show a simple example that captures the main idea of the paper. (see figure: Effect of translation on the wavelet representation of a signal (caption and figure after @Simoncelli92. (a) An input signal. (b-d) The high-, mid-, and low-frequency coefficients within a wavelet...) The figure above from a different paper conveys a main idea very simply. The paper's main idea was that wavelets lacked important desirable features for an image representation. @fig-wavelet shows the failure of a wavelet representation to form a translation invariant representation. The top row shows two versions of the same signal, differing only in a one-sample translation. The bottom three rows show the coefficients of the high-, mid-, and low-frequency bands of a wavelet representation of that signal. The figure points out in a simple way the drawback of a wavelet representation with aliased subbands that was the focus of the paper: as the signal translates, the signal representation energy moves to different frequency bands and changes form within the mid-frequency band.
concepts.motivation_md: Visualizations allow readers to grasp complex technical arguments quickly through concrete examples, making the paper's core thesis more accessible and memorable.
concepts.recap_md: - Use simple examples to visually capture the paper's main idea.

concepts.title: Experimental evidence in research papers
concepts.one_liner: Modern standards require that assertions in a research paper be backed up with quantitative experimental evidence.
concepts.content: In earlier days of computer vision research, good ideas could be presented with only plausibility arguments to support them. However, modern standards require that assertions in a paper be backed up with experimental evidence. Readers will be expecting a table quantitatively comparing the performance of your algorithm with that of the previous state-of-the-art. If you are proposing a new task for which there aren't previous benchmarks, you should still compare with an algorithm that solves a related task, noting that the algorithm was designed for a different task. (see figure: prototypical table of results, from \cite{Owens2016} Rows are different algorithms, or ablations of a favored algorithm. Columns are datasets or tasks, and the numbers indicate performance, with the...)
concepts.motivation_md: Plausibility arguments are no longer sufficient in modern research; quantitative comparisons provide the objective proof needed to validate a new algorithm's effectiveness against existing methods.
concepts.recap_md: - Back up all claims with experimental evidence and quantitative data.

concepts.title: Strategies for ending a paper
concepts.one_liner: Instead of listing unfinished work, a paper should end by reviewing contributions and emphasizing how the research changes the field.
concepts.content: You should resist the temptation to describe the items that were left unfinished in a section on "Future Work." It is hard to imagine a weaker way to end the paper than to enumerate all the things the paper doesn't accomplish, providing a summary of where it falls short. Instead, the paper can finish with a review of what has been presented, emphasizing the contributions. How has the world changed, now that the reader has read this paper? What new research directions have been opened up; what can we do now that we couldn't do before?
concepts.motivation_md: Ending on a list of failures or uncompleted tasks leaves the reader with a negative impression. A strong conclusion reinforces the paper's value and its impact on future research.
concepts.recap_md: - Avoid ending with a "Future Work" section that highlights shortcomings.

concepts.title: Reader-centric writing principle
concepts.one_liner: The most important principle of good writing is to keep the reader uppermost in mind, anticipating their needs and expectations.
concepts.content: Donald Knuth wrote, "Perhaps the most important principle of good writing is to keep the reader uppermost in mind: What does the reader know so far? What does the reader expect next and why?" Our mental image is that of a great host, who anticipates every need of their house guest. At every moment, they know what you might be wanting and how to help you find it.
concepts.motivation_md: Writing is a form of communication; by anticipating the reader's questions and knowledge level, the author ensures the information is transmitted effectively and clearly.
concepts.recap_md: - Always consider what the reader knows and what they expect next.

concepts.title: Concise writing principle
concepts.one_liner: Vigorous writing is concise, containing no unnecessary words or sentences to ensure clarity and respect page limits.
concepts.content: In *The Elements of Style*, Strunk and White write, "Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences, for the same reason that a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts." Writing more concisely helps your paper in two ways. First, researchers are typically fighting against a page limit, particularly in conference submissions, so tighter text lets the author say more or add another figure. Second, concise text is usually clearer and easier to understand.
concepts.motivation_md: Conciseness improves readability and allows authors to fit more information into the strict page limits common in scientific publishing.
concepts.recap_md: - Eliminate unnecessary words and sentences to improve clarity.

concepts.title: Reader engagement and skimming
concepts.one_liner: Since many readers only skim papers, the title, figures, and abstract must be self-contained to convey the top-level message.
concepts.content: While we may imagine our reader reading every word of our paper, in our current era of many published papers, most of your readers will probably only skim your paper. (see figure: The conjectured readership of a computer science paper (conjectured relative amounts). Many people will read the title, but far fewer will read the abstract or look at the figures. Fewer still will...) You should write your paper so that readers will learn from it, even at reduced levels of engagement. The title should convey the top-level message of the paper. The figures and their captions should be self-contained and tell the story of the paper. The abstract should provide a good summary.
concepts.motivation_md: In a high-volume publishing environment, authors must optimize for skimmers to ensure their core message reaches the widest possible audience.
concepts.recap_md: - Design titles, figures, and abstracts to be informative even when skimmed.

concepts.title: Self-contained figure captions
concepts.one_liner: Figure captions should be self-contained so that readers can understand the main takeaway without reading the full paper.
concepts.content: Because you can assume that many of the readers of your figure captions will not be reading the full paper, the captions should be self-contained. They should point out what readers are supposed to notice about the figure, to help both the full-paper reader and the figures-only reader. (see figure: Figure and caption from \cite{FreemanShapetime}. The caption should be understandable by itself, and should point to what the reader should take away from the figure.)
concepts.motivation_md: Many readers browse figures before (or instead of) reading the text; self-contained captions ensure these readers still grasp the paper's key evidence and results.
concepts.recap_md: - Write captions that explain the figure's significance independently of the main text.

concepts.title: Writing with equations
concepts.one_liner: Your sentences should flow smoothly when all but the simplest formulas are replaced by 'blah' or some other grunting noise.
concepts.content: Equations interposed with text can pose a challenge to the reader, who must decide whether to stop to work through each equation or continue reading as if the equations were words. To address this, your sentences should flow smoothly even when complex formulas are replaced by a placeholder like "blah." Additionally, when referring to an equation, identify it by a descriptive phrase as well as a number. For example, instead of merely saying "inserting (2.47) and (3.51) into (5.13)," it is more helpful to say "inserting the form (2.47) of the electric field $E$ and the Lindhard form (3.51) of the dielectric function $\epsilon$ into the constitutive equation (5.13)."
concepts.motivation_md: Mathematical notation can disrupt the narrative flow of a technical paper. These guidelines ensure that readers can follow the logical argument of a text without being forced to decode every complex equation on their first pass.
concepts.recap_md:
- Ensure sentences remain grammatically coherent even if formulas are ignored.
 - Identify equations by both their reference number and a descriptive phrase.

concepts.title: Tone in scientific writing
concepts.one_liner: Develop a reputation for being clear and reliable by maintaining a generous, honest, and accurate tone in your writing.
concepts.content: The tone of your writing is critical; you should resist the pressure to oversell results, hide drawbacks, or disparage the work of others. If your work has a shortcoming, it is better to point it out yourself than to have someone else discover it later. Adopting a generous tone—viewing colleagues as good researchers doing their best—promotes long-lasting professional relationships and wins over readers. You should aim for a reputation of clarity and reliability by always conveying an accurate impression of an algorithm's performance. If a method fails in important cases, inform the reader, as documenting counterintuitive results or failures can prove valuable to the field in the long term.
concepts.motivation_md: Maintaining a professional and honest tone builds credibility with the scientific community and prevents future embarrassment when limitations are inevitably discovered.
concepts.recap_md:
- Be honest about shortcomings and failures in your own work.
 - Use a generous tone toward other researchers to build professional goodwill.
 - Prioritize accuracy and reliability over overselling your results.

concepts.title: Relationship between paper quality and impact
concepts.one_liner: Only high-quality papers significantly impact a research career, so prioritize quality over quantity.
concepts.content:
While the number of papers is a rough measure of productivity, in the eyes of mentors, search committees, and managers, only the good papers count. This relationship is illustrated in @fig-impact, which shows that only high-quality papers have a significant impact on one's career. Therefore, it is essential to learn how to write the best possible paper from any given piece of research.

(see figure: Plot of conjectured data showing the impact of a paper on one's career, as a function of paper quality.)
concepts.motivation_md: Students often feel pressured to publish frequently, but a resume full of mediocre papers is less effective than one with a few truly excellent contributions.
concepts.recap_md: - Focus on making every paper as good as possible rather than just increasing your paper count.

concepts.title: Standard paper organization structure
concepts.one_liner: A standard research paper structure moves from problem definition and existing solutions to your own method and results.
concepts.content:
A successful research paper typically follows a specific logical progression:

- Start by stating the problem and why the audience should care about it.
- Briefly state existing solutions and explain why they are unsatisfactory.
- Explain your own solution, compare it to others, and demonstrate why it is better.
- Conclude by discussing related work that uses similar techniques for different problems.

This structure often maps to standard section headings: Introduction, Related Work, Main Idea, Algorithm (with specific sub-steps), Experiments, and Discussion.
concepts.motivation_md: Standardized organization helps readers quickly find information and understand the value proposition of the research relative to existing work.
concepts.recap_md: - Clearly state the problem and why existing solutions fail before presenting your own.

prereq.rationale: Concise writing is motivated by the reader-centric goal of making text clearer and easier to understand.
Understanding the reality of reader skimming is a prerequisite for applying the reader-centric principle effectively in modern scientific publishing.
The requirement for self-contained captions is a direct consequence of the observation that many readers only look at figures and captions.
The 'blah' test is a specific technique used to ensure that mathematical notation does not disrupt the reader's narrative flow.
The introduction is the first component of the standard paper organization, and its success is defined by how well it sets up that structure.
Visualizing the main idea is a specific technique for the 'Main Idea' section of the standard paper structure.
The requirement for experimental evidence dictates the content and necessity of the 'Experiments' section in the standard structure.
This strategy defines how to effectively execute the final section of the standard paper organization structure.

overlay.rationale: Both concepts emphasize making the core message accessible to readers who may not read the entire text through visual and structural cues.
The way a paper is organized and presented directly influences its quality and subsequent impact on the field.
